passage:
Wednesday night
Hafsa from final year sat with me at lunch again. She said I'm "so much more mature than the other first-years", that I have "leader energy", that she could tell the first time she saw me. I felt ten feet tall.
Then she told me about the "opportunity": sell some products, bring in two friends, pay a joining fee, "and you'll earn more than your parents". She said, "Someone like you won't overthink it."
The weird part: I wanted to say yes just so I wouldn't seem rude after all those compliments. Saying "let me think" felt like slapping her.
But I did say it. Tonight I'm asking my brother, and I'll look the company up on a consumer forum before I pay anything. If it's real, it'll still be real on Monday.
Amandeep

qa.q: What did Hafsa say Amandeep has?
qa.a: "Leader energy", and she said Amandeep is "so much more mature than the other first-years".

qa.q: Why did saying "let me think" feel so hard for Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep felt flattered and warm, then awkward, because after so many compliments disagreeing felt rude, like slapping Hafsa.

qa.q: What protective steps does Amandeep plan?
qa.a: Amandeep will pause, ask the brother tonight, and look the company up on a consumer forum before paying anything.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's "Someone like you won't overthink it" suggest about what she wants?
qa.a: It suggests she wants a quick yes and is using flattery to discourage careful thinking.

grounding: A young adult receiving lavish praise from someone with a pitch feels warm and finds that disagreeing now feels rude, but pauses to check.

passage:
Store supervisor's note, Friday. Written by Manjula, inventory team.
Aadhya, our summer intern, has been checking deliveries this month. Today a vendor's representative spent ten minutes praising her. "You're the sharpest person here. Your seniors are lucky. Honestly, you're wasted in a stockroom." Aadhya was smiling, clearly pleased.
Then he said, "The count's fine, na? We're in a rush." And she signed without opening the last four boxes. When I asked about it afterward, she said, "It felt rude to question him after he was so nice."
I didn't scold her. I told her that's exactly how flattery works: once someone makes you feel special, disagreeing feels like bad manners. We opened the four boxes together. Two were short.
She was upset. I said it happens to everyone, even me. From Monday, every delivery gets counted, however friendly the driver is.

qa.q: How many of the last four boxes were short?
qa.a: Two were short.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the representative praised her?
qa.a: Aadhya felt pleased and special, which made her less careful and uncomfortable about questioning him.

qa.q: What did the supervisor put in place from Monday?
qa.a: Every delivery gets counted, however friendly the driver is, so the check doesn't depend on how someone makes you feel.

qa.q: How might the vendor's representative have seen the praise?
qa.a: He likely used it as a tool to hurry Aadhya past the count, knowing praise makes disagreement feel rude.

grounding: A supervisor records a young intern who, after lavish praise from a vendor, felt special and lowered her guard on the delivery count.

passage:
Sunday, late
Ganga Di, the senior in the next room, stopped by again tonight. She read my story for the college magazine and said I'm the best writer she's seen in years. That I have "a real voice." That I remind her of herself.
I felt like I was glowing. Nobody has ever said that to me.
Then she said, "You'd be so good at the history assignment too. Can you write mine? You write so fast. It would take you an hour."
I said yes before I could think. Saying no felt so rude, after everything she'd just said.
Now I'm lying here and my stomach feels strange. It's copying. If it's caught, we're both in trouble. And she didn't ask about my story at all after that.
Tomorrow I'll tell her I can't. I'll say I'll help her plan it, not write it. My hands are cold just thinking about it.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Ganga Di ask Sabina to write?
qa.a: She asked Sabina to write her history assignment.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after saying yes?
qa.a: Sabina felt uneasy and anxious, her stomach strange, realising the praise had made it hard to say no.

qa.q: What does Sabina plan to do tomorrow?
qa.a: Sabina plans to tell Ganga Di she can't write it, but can help her plan it instead.

qa.q: How might Ganga Di react to Sabina's refusal?
qa.a: Ganga Di might feel annoyed or disappointed at first, since she was counting on the praise to get a yes.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult feeling special after lavish praise and dropping caution about a request she should have refused.

passage: The dust had just settled from the evening bus when Kiran walked into the little agri-shop in the kasba with a box of sweets. "Vijay-ji, the whole block talks about you," he said. "So young and running this shop better than men twice your age. Farmers trust only you." Vijay felt his ears warm. Nobody had called him Vijay-ji before. Kiran spread out glossy leaflets for a new seed variety and a stock agreement. "For a smart man like you, it's just a signature." Vijay picked up the pen. Questions rose in his mind about trials and which farmers had used it, but asking felt rude after such kindness. Then his father's old diary on the counter caught his eye, full of crossed-out company names. Vijay put the pen down. "Leave the papers. I'll read them with Bapu tonight." Kiran's smile tightened for a second.

qa.q: What did Kiran bring when he walked into the shop?
qa.a: Kiran brought a box of sweets.

qa.q: Why did asking questions feel hard for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay felt flattered and warm at being called Vijay-ji, so questioning Kiran felt rude and awkward after such kindness.

qa.q: What protective step did Vijay take, and why does it help?
qa.a: He put the pen down and kept the papers to read with Bapu that night, which gave him time and a second person away from the praise.

qa.q: What might Kiran's tightened smile suggest about how he sees the delay?
qa.a: It may suggest Kiran was counting on a quick signature and saw the pause as a setback, though a smile alone cannot prove what he intended.

grounding: Shows a young shopkeeper whose guard drops under lavish praise from someone who wants a signature, making questions feel rude.
